questions.q: Why doesn't a bare SELECT inside an Oracle procedure return a result set the way it does in T-SQL?
options: Oracle procedures don't auto-stream a SELECT's results back to the caller; there's no built-in equivalent of T-SQL's behavior
Oracle procedures can never contain a SELECT statement
Oracle requires every SELECT to be wrapped in DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE
A bare SELECT in Oracle automatically becomes a REF CURSOR with no extra syntax
questions.explain: T-SQL streams a procedure's bare SELECT back to the caller automatically. Oracle has no such behavior, which is exactly the gap REF CURSORs fill.

options: A cursor variable that can be opened for different queries at runtime and passed around
A fixed, named cursor whose query is set once at declaration and can never change
A synonym for DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE
A package-level session-persistent variable
questions.explain: Unlike an ordinary explicit cursor bound to one fixed query, a REF CURSOR is a variable you OPEN FOR any query at runtime.

options: Oracle's generic, weakly-typed ref cursor data type, usable for any query shape
A system table that logs every cursor ever opened
A T-SQL data type with no Oracle equivalent
A strongly-typed cursor that can only be opened for one specific query
questions.explain: SYS_REFCURSOR is the generic ref cursor type most developers reach for because it's flexible enough to be opened for any query.

questions.q: How does an Oracle procedure hand a result set back to its caller?
options: Give it an OUT parameter typed SYS_REFCURSOR and OPEN it FOR the query inside the procedure
Use a bare SELECT with no special handling, exactly like T-SQL
Wrap the query in an EXCEPTION block
Declare the result set as a package-level variable
questions.explain: The OUT SYS_REFCURSOR parameter, opened for a query inside the procedure, is Oracle's direct equivalent of what T-SQL gives you for free.

questions.q: What can the SAME REF CURSOR variable do that an ordinary named cursor cannot?
options: Be opened for entirely different queries at runtime depending on logic, since its query isn't fixed at declaration time
Run without ever being closed
Return more than one result set simultaneously
Skip the FETCH step entirely
questions.explain: Because it's a variable, a REF CURSOR can be opened for different queries depending on runtime conditions — a named cursor's query is fixed at declaration.
